beginner: Cilantro likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost mixed in that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy, but steady moisture and rich soil keep the leaves tender and mild and put off bolting a little; hot, dry, hard soil makes it rush to flower and turn the foliage bitter.
seasoned: Cilantro grows in most soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Utah State University suggests working 2 to 4 inches of well-rotted compost into the top 4 to 6 inches before sowing, which feeds the fast leaf growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and slow to bolt. It dislikes damp, humid, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off and leaf disease. The plant has a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

beginner: Cilantro grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.2 to 6.8. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.2 to 6.8, slightly acidic to neutral; cilantro is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 6.0 to 7.5. Clemson lists a working range of 6 to 7 for the crop. It is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Cilantro grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding once the seedlings are up and growing. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again, and a plant left to make coriander seed needs nothing more.
seasoned: Cilantro is a fast leafy herb that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that a modest charge is plenty. Utah State University suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, one to two times during the season. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen once the seedlings are established to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy late nitrogen, which draws aphids and does little for a crop you cut within a few weeks; a plant grown on for coriander seed needs no extra feeding once it bolts.

beginner: Time to give your cilantro a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cilantro with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once or twice while the plants are young.
seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal once or twice during the crop. No extra phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 4-to-6-week leaf crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding while the plants are young.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, side-dressed once or twice during the crop; a compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach and other aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Cilantro's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on cilantro; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Pick the leaves before a colony settles in.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which cilantro's own flowers attract.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and pick the quick crop young.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and harvest the fast crop before colonies build; letting a few plants flower draws in aphid predators.

beginner: Small wedge-shaped insects that hop or fly up when disturbed, plus yellowed, twisted, or stunted plants. The leafhoppers themselves do little chewing damage, but they can carry diseases that deform the plant.
seasoned: The beet leafhopper and aster leafhoppers feed on cilantro and, more importantly, transmit aster yellows and beet curly top virus, which yellow, distort, and stunt the plants. Infected plants do not recover and should be removed.

beginner: Tiny jumping insects that suck sap and, more seriously, spread diseases (aster yellows and curly top) that twist and yellow the plants.
seasoned: Leafhoppers (including the beet leafhopper, Circulifer tenellus) feed on the foliage and vector aster yellows and beet curly top virus; the disease damage far outweighs the feeding.

beginner: Cover plants with a light row cover to keep leafhoppers off, pull and discard any yellowed, distorted plants right away, and clear nearby weeds that harbor the insects and the diseases.
seasoned: Exclude leafhoppers with floating row cover, rogue out symptomatic plants promptly since there is no cure for the viral diseases, and control weed reservoirs; insecticides give poor control of a mobile vector.

beginner: Use row cover, clear weedy hosts around the garden, and remove infected plants early so they do not seed disease into the planting.
seasoned: Manage leafhoppers mainly by exclusion (row cover) and sanitation: remove weed reservoirs and rogue symptomatic plants, since spraying rarely stops a mobile virus vector.

beginner: Small dark, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that run along the veins and can merge into larger blotches, worst in cool, wet weather. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Angular, vein-limited dark lesions on the foliage, sometimes with a yellow halo, spreading in cool, wet, splashy conditions; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the harvest. It is the most-reported cilantro disease.

beginner: A bacterial disease, the most common one reported on cilantro, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and often arrives on infected seed.
seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. coriandricola, a seed-borne and splash-spread bacterium favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free or hot-water-treated seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from cilantro and its relatives, and remove infected debris; copper has limited effect once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the bacterium over.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where cilantro's slow germination leaves seed sitting.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting cilantro seed sits a long time before emerging.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows cilantro's already slow germination favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed; some growers soak the dry seed to speed emergence past the vulnerable window.

beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and stems, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most common fungal disease of cilantro, that builds in warm days with cool nights and crowded plantings; coated leaves lose quality.

beginner: A fungal disease (Erysiphe heraclei) that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, and crowding.
seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe heraclei, favored by warm days and cool humid nights and by dense stands with poor airflow.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding. Most home crops are harvested before it does much harm.
seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, and avoid excess nitrogen; the fast leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a plant grown on for seed is more exposed.

beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and pick the leaf crop young before mildew builds.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for coriander seed.

beginner: Mushy, slimy, foul-smelling collapse of the crown or stems, usually in warm, wet conditions or after the foliage has been damaged. Affected plants rot quickly.
seasoned: Wet, mushy breakdown of the crown and stems with a bad smell, caused by soft-rot bacteria entering through wounds in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions; the plant collapses fast.

beginner: Bacterial soft rot that enters through wounds and rots the tissue in warm, wet, poorly drained soil.
seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (such as Pectobacterium species) invade through wounds and bruises and dissolve the tissue, favored by warm temperatures, wet soil, and poor drainage.

beginner: Remove and discard rotted plants, improve drainage, avoid injuring the plants, and do not overwater. There is no cure once a plant is rotting.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants, improve drainage and airflow, avoid wounding and overwatering, and do not work the bed when wet; no rescue once rot sets in.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, avoid overwatering and injury, and keep the planting open so foliage dries.
seasoned: Site in well-drained soil, avoid waterlogging and mechanical injury, space for drying airflow, and clear infected debris.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; cilantro is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns harsher under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; Texas A&M notes an inch a week suffices once established unless it turns very hot.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks bacterial leaf spot and other leaf diseases on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mushy or diseased in soggy soil.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and soft rot or leaf disease in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, harsher-tasting leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its coriander seedstalk.

beginner: Cilantro is slow to sprout, so keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: Cilantro germinates slowly, so keep the seedbed evenly moist through emergence; steady moisture here is the first step in delaying the eventual bolt.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered. Cilantro has shallow roots and dries out quickly.
seasoned: Grow the shallow-rooted seedlings on with steady, even moisture; they show stress fast.

beginner: Keep the water steady, about an inch a week and more when warm. Even moisture keeps cilantro mild and tender and holds off bolting; letting it get dry and hot sends it straight to flower and coarsens the leaves. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Cilantro is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns harsher under drought, so keep an even inch a week, more in warm spells (TAMU notes an inch a week suffices unless it turns very hot). Even moisture keeps it growing fast, tender, and mild and delays the bolt; water at the soil line to keep the lacy foliage dry against bacterial leaf spot.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you cut. A dry, hot spell now makes cilantro bolt and turn bitter fast, so steady water keeps the leaves coming a little longer.
seasoned: Keep even moisture right through the cutting weeks: any dry, hot check hurries the plant to flower and makes the leaves harsh, so steady water buys more tender leaf before it bolts.

beginner: When cilantro bolts and runs to seed, the leaves are done. Water less now, and if you want coriander seed, a dry finish helps it ripen on the plant.
seasoned: Once cilantro bolts and heads to coriander seed the leaf crop is over; ease off watering, and if you want the coriander seed, a drier finish helps it ripen and dry down on the plant.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps cilantro growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it straight to flower and coriander seed and coarsen the leaves.

beginner: Plant cilantro straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since the plants handle frost. The seeds are slow, often taking one to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt almost right away. A summer crop is really for the coriander seed.
seasoned: Cilantro is almost always direct-sown, since it has a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost, and it germinates slowly, often 7 to 21 days. The round seed is actually two seeds fused, so growers sometimes gently crack it to speed and even out germination. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to taste. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since heat both slows germination and bolts the crop almost at once; midsummer sowings are grown for coriander seed rather than leaves.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter, deep enough for cilantro's taproot.

beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a little starter nitrogen; cilantro is a quick feeder but needs only a light charge for its short leaf life.

beginner: Pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist, since drought makes cilantro bolt.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts cilantro.

beginner: Feed a little, since watering washes nutrients out of pots, but the crop is so fast it rarely needs more than a starter charge.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown cilantro can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since cilantro takes frost. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring before bolting.
seasoned: Cilantro is frost-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and giving the earliest, longest leaf run before spring heat bolts it. In cold zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; a hard freeze will still kill it.

beginner: Cilantro is an easy, fast container herb. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep to fit its root, sow the seed thickly, and snip leaves cut-and-come-again. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.
seasoned: Cilantro grows well in a container at least 8 inches deep to fit its taproot, sown densely for cut-and-come-again leaves. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns, and to keep a fresh succession by the kitchen door.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits cilantro well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves mild and slow to bolt.

seasoned: Cilantro has a slender taproot, so give it depth: a container at least 8 inches deep suits it better than a shallow tray, while width adds sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves.

beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, dill, fennel, celery, parsnip, and cilantro itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leafhopper-vectored aster yellows, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow cilantro or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant cilantro after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Cilantro often self-sows, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.
seasoned: Rotate cilantro and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share aster yellows (spread by leafhoppers), the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow cilantro with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because cilantro readily self-sows from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place.

beginner: Cilantro flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn bitter. To keep the leaves coming, grow it in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, give afternoon shade when it is warm, and try slow-bolting types like Santo or Calypso. When it does bolt, do not fight it: let the plant flower and make coriander seed, which is the spice.
seasoned: Cilantro bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter as it shifts to its coriander seedstalk. Keep the leaf window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, which is the longer and more reliable leaf season, choose slow-bolting types (Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Slow Bolting) where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. There is no real fix once it bolts, so the productive answer in heat is to stop fighting it and grow the plant on for coriander seed.

beginner: Cilantro bolts (sends up a flower stalk) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast, but it is not a mistake: the very same flowering that ends the leafy cilantro gives you coriander seed, the spice. The flowers are great for bees and helpful insects, and the plant often drops seed and comes up again on its own. Grow it in cool weather for leaves, and let it bloom in summer for seed.
seasoned: Bolting in cilantro is driven by heat above roughly 75°F and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. This is the defining fact of the crop: the same bolt that ends the cilantro leaf harvest begins the coriander seed crop, so the plant is not failing, it is changing product. The white flowers feed pollinators and beneficial insects strongly, and bolted plants self-sow readily. In hot regions the leaf window is short and growers deliberately let summer plantings run to coriander seed.

beginner: Do not leave cut cilantro out on the counter, where it wilts fast; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water. Dried coriander seed keeps for months at room temperature.
seasoned: Fresh cilantro leaves wilt within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days. Coriander seed, by contrast, is shelf-stable for months once dried.

beginner: Store fresh cilantro unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh leaves unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; cilantro holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Cilantro does not freeze well for salads, but you can chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze that for cooking. For coriander, let the seeds dry on the plant, then store them in a jar.
seasoned: Fresh cilantro loses its texture frozen for raw use, but freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or blended into sauces, where the flavor holds for cooking. Coriander seed is dried, not frozen: cut seed heads as they brown, dry them, then thresh and store the seed airtight.

beginner: Use fresh cilantro within a week or so of picking, since it does not keep long. Coriander seed is the opposite: dry the brown seed heads, shake out the seeds, and store them in a sealed jar for many months.
seasoned: Cilantro is best straight from the garden, delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week; its flavor is also strongest fresh. The seed is the keeper: harvest coriander when the seed heads turn tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, and the threshed seed stores airtight for months to a year.

beginner: If you want leaves, pick a slow-bolting cilantro like Santo, Calypso, Leisure, or one labeled Slow Bolting or Long Standing, which take a bit longer to flower. None of them stop flowering in heat, so sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks too. If you want coriander seed, just let any cilantro flower and go to seed.
seasoned: Match the type to the goal. For leaves, choose slow-bolting selections, Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Caribe, and the various Slow Bolting and Long Standing strains, which hold in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; none truly resist heat and long days, but they buy time. Specialty leaf types include Delfino, a feathery cut-leaf cilantro, and Lemon. For coriander seed, any standard cilantro left to bolt sets seed readily, and large-seeded types like Moroccan are grown specifically for the spice. Because the bolt is inevitable, succession sowing matters more than variety for a steady leaf supply.

beginner: Cilantro is small, fast, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes when it flowers: the blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with quick cool-season greens like lettuce and spinach, and with legumes. Keep it away from fennel, a poor neighbor for most herbs that can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants.
seasoned: Most cilantro companion value is real but indirect: allowed to flower, cilantro (an Apiaceae umbel) is a strong insectary plant, recruiting hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids and caterpillars on neighboring crops, an effect extension IPM guidance leans on. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which benefit from those beneficials and lend the cool-season cilantro a little afternoon shade), with quick cool greens that share its season, and with legumes. The well-grounded caution is fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor that also crosses with carrot-family plants. Avoid clustering cilantro with its Apiaceae relatives (carrot, dill, parsley) on rotation and shared-pest grounds.

beginner: Let some cilantro flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and caterpillars. The taller plants also give cilantro a little cooling shade in warm weather.
seasoned: A beneficial-insect pairing: cilantro left to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and hornworms on tomatoes and peppers, and the taller crops shade the cool-season cilantro to slow its bolt. Sound by mechanism and shared culture, not a measured cilantro-tomato effect.

beginner: Lettuce and spinach grow fast and low in the same cool weather as cilantro, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed.
seasoned: A cool-season interplant on space and timing: cilantro, lettuce, and spinach share a cool window and a salad bed and are cut young together, with no shared major pest. Traditional and structural rather than a documented effect.

beginner: Legumes add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy cilantro can use, and they share a cool-to-mild season without crowding it.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans and peas fix a little nitrogen the leafy cilantro draws on, and the quick cilantro uses the open ground between them. Sound space-and-timing logic, not a measured cilantro effect.

beginner: Keep cilantro away from fennel. Fennel is a poor neighbor for most herbs and vegetables, said to release substances that hold back nearby plants, and it can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants like cilantro if both flower.
seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and the classic bad herb neighbor, releasing compounds that suppress many plants, and as a fellow Apiaceae it can cross-pollinate cilantro where both flower for seed. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured cilantro-fennel trial.

beginner: The first thin little leaves poking up. Cilantro is slow, often taking one to three weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
seasoned: The first pair of narrow seed leaves pushing up. Cilantro is slow to germinate, often 7 to 21 days, and emergence can be uneven because each round fruit holds two seeds.

beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings are up, which can take a couple of weeks. Sow in cool weather, not summer heat.
seasoned: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Sow into cool soil; warm soil above about 75°F slows germination and primes early bolting.

beginner: Any sprouts yet?
seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: The first true leaves, the broad lacy cilantro leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
seasoned: The first true leaves, the broad, scalloped lower cilantro leaves. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.

beginner: Thin the seedlings, leaving them close for cutting leaves or farther apart for bigger plants, and eat the ones you pull. Keep the water steady.
seasoned: Thin to taste, dense at 2 to 4 inches for cut leaf or 6 to 8 inches for fuller plants, and eat the thinnings. Keep moisture steady to delay the bolt.

beginner: How are they coming along?
seasoned: How are they coming along?

beginner: Leafy plants a few inches tall and full enough to start picking, before any flower stalk appears.
seasoned: Leafy plants 4 to 6 inches tall and the patch looking full, well before any central stalk rises. This is the short, productive leaf window.

beginner: Start picking the outer leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
seasoned: Start cutting outer leaves or shearing now rather than waiting; regular light cutting keeps tender new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.

beginner: Ready to start cutting?
seasoned: Ready to start cutting?

beginner: Full, tender leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a stalk appears the good leaf window is closing fast.
seasoned: Full, tender leaves with no central flower stalk yet. Once a feathery stalk rises the leaf window is closing fast and the lower leaves coarsen.

beginner: Take the outer leaves, or cut the patch a couple of inches above the soil so it regrows. Pick young in the cool morning, and once you see a flower stalk either clear it or let it go to coriander seed.
seasoned: Cut outer leaves or shear the patch a couple of inches above the crown for regrowth. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear or convert a patch to seed as soon as it shows a stalk.

beginner: Harvesting regularly?
seasoned: Harvesting regularly?

beginner: A tall feathery stalk from the middle, then white flowers and round green seeds. This is cilantro turning into coriander, and it happens fast.
seasoned: A feathery central stalk shooting up, the new leaves narrowing into thread-like fronds, then white umbel flowers and green seed. This is the shift from cilantro leaf to coriander seed, and it is rapid.

beginner: If you want leaves, pick everything good right away. If you want coriander seed, leave the plant to flower and set seed, then cut and dry the brown seed heads. Cilantro often reseeds itself too.
seasoned: For leaves, harvest everything worth eating at once. To make coriander, leave the plant: let the flowers feed pollinators, then cut the seed heads as they turn tan but before they shatter, and dry them. Let one plant self-sow if you want volunteers.

beginner: Cilantro and coriander come from the very same plant: the leaves are cilantro and the dried seeds are the spice coriander. Unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, cilantro is a cool-weather plant that handles frost but bolts (flowers) very fast once it gets warm, above about 75°F, and the leaves turn bitter. So the trick is to grow it in the cool parts of the year: a short spring window, a longer and better fall crop, and overwintering in mild areas. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, since each plant bolts after a few weeks, and plant the seeds right in the garden because cilantro does not like being moved. It is fast and easy, with baby leaves in about 3 to 4 weeks. And when summer heat finally makes it bolt, do not be discouraged: let it flower and you get coriander seed.
seasoned: Cilantro and coriander are one plant, Coriandrum sativum, an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) grown for two products: the leaf is the herb cilantro and the dried seed is the spice coriander. Its defining biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil: cilantro is a COOL-season, frost-tolerant crop that bolts almost the moment the weather warms, sending up a flower stalk above roughly 75°F and with lengthening days. That single fact shapes everything. The spring leaf window is short, fall is the main and most reliable leaf season, and in mild zones a fall sowing overwinters for the earliest, longest spring run; in hot regions and the heat of summer the leaf crop is brief and growers instead let the plant bolt and harvest coriander seed. Because the bolt is fast and inevitable, cilantro is a succession crop above all, sown in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks so a fresh, pre-bolt cohort is always coming on. It is direct-sown (a slender taproot resents transplanting), fast (baby leaf in about 3 to 4 weeks, bolting by 45 to 60 days), and easy, with few serious pests. The grower's real skill is timing the crop into the cool shoulders of the year and accepting the bolt as the start of the coriander harvest rather than a failure.

beginner: Start picking cilantro when the plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, a few weeks after sowing and before you see a flower stalk. seasoned: Begin cutting cilantro leaves once plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, roughly 3 to 6 weeks from sowing, well before any central stalk rises. Cut the broad lower leaves, or shear the whole patch a couple of inches above the crown for a second cutting, taking no more than a third at a time and picking in the cool morning for the mildest flavor. Pick promptly and often as the weather warms, since the leaf window closes fast at bolt. For coriander, stop cutting and let the plant flower and set seed; harvest the seed heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, then thresh and store the seed airtight.
